author: BrentDesk Staff
headline: Culinary talent development features at Riyadh hospitality summit
deck: Culinary talent development is a declared theme of the Riyadh hospitality summit, with training institutions on the speaker list alongside the chefs.
excerpt: Culinary talent development features as a declared theme at the Riyadh hospitality summit, with training academies sharing a speaker list with executive chefs from Hilton and Hyatt.
content:
Among the declared themes of the Hospitality Leaders Summit at Riyadh's hotel exhibition from 15 September is culinary talent development, and the speaker list attached to it is unusually weighted toward the problem.

The chefs are there: Bilal Saleh, regional chef for Hilton in Saudi Arabia; Omar Alazeeh, executive chef at Hyatt Place AlUla; Felipe Alvear, culinary director at Grand Hyatt The Red Sea; and Daniele Chiari, culinary director at Royal Protocol Hospitality and Catering. So are the trainers: Dr Jorge Arnanz, executive director of the academy at King Faisal International Academy; Amna Alyamani, director of the culinary centre at Alkhaleej Training and Education; and Hakim Bagabas, director of culinary at Food Passion ME.

Putting operators and training institutions on the same platform reflects a straightforward arithmetic problem. Saudi Arabia is carrying a hotel pipeline of roughly 99,500 rooms against an existing base near 167,500 keys, weighted heavily toward the premium tier. Premium hotels run full-service food and beverage operations, and a full-service kitchen at that standard requires a brigade of trained cooks under a chef with years of experience — not a headcount that can be recruited at short notice or trained in a season.

The constraint is the same one that recurs across this month's coverage in other sectors: physical capability can be built quickly, judgement cannot. A kitchen can be equipped in weeks, as the co-located SaudiHost exhibition demonstrates. Staffing it with people who can run it to a brand standard through a full occupancy cycle takes years, and the training pipeline has to have started well before the building opened.

Nationalisation policy sharpens it. Hospitality has historically drawn on expatriate labour across the Gulf, and Saudi employment targets apply to the sector as they do elsewhere. That means the pipeline must produce Saudi nationals in numbers and at a skill level the industry has not previously required domestically, which is precisely why formal academies rather than in-house training appear on this platform.

The commercial stakes are larger than staffing costs suggest. Food and beverage as a growth driver is a separate declared theme of the same summit, reflecting a regional reassessment of hotel F&B from a cost centre justified by guest expectation into a revenue line in its own right. A hotel restaurant that draws local custom rather than only residents is a different business, and it depends entirely on the kitchen being good enough to compete with standalone restaurants.

Osamah Mohamed Ali Alawwam of Roasting House Commercial Company and Ali Safa of Costa Coffee Professional appear on the same list from the beverage side, alongside the CoffeeZone programme running on the floor.

Speaker names and titles are taken from the organiser's published summit page.
